title: IF JESUS FULFILLED THE LAW, WHY DO BIBLICAL SEXUAL LAWS STILL FEEL SO PERSONAL?
paragraphs: IF JESUS FULFILLED THE LAW, WHY DO BIBLICAL SEXUAL LAWS STILL FEEL SO PERSONAL?

The uncomfortable question many Christians quietly ask: If we are under grace, not the Mosaic covenant, what exactly does Jesus expect us to do with the Bible’s sexual boundaries—and what happens when those boundaries reach into the most private room of our lives?
There is a moment when Christianity stops being theoretical.
It usually does not happen while you are sitting comfortably in church.
It happens when Scripture touches something you love.
Something you want.
Something you have already justified.

Something connected to your body, your relationship, your memories, your loneliness, your marriage, your attraction, your secret browser history, your private conversations, your past, your shame—or the person you cannot imagine surrendering.
Suddenly the Bible is no longer an ancient book sitting politely on a shelf.
It is standing in your bedroom.
And that is when one of the most emotionally loaded questions in Christianity comes crawling out of the shadows:
“If Jesus fulfilled the Law, why should Christians still care about biblical sexual laws?”
Maybe you have wondered it.
Maybe somebody you love has asked it.
Maybe you have heard someone say:
“Christians eat pork.”
“Christians wear mixed fabrics.”
“Christians do not offer animal sacrifices.”
“So why do Christians suddenly quote the Old Testament when sex enters the conversation?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves more than outrage.
And it certainly deserves more than Christians throwing isolated Bible verses at hurting people as though winning an argument were the same thing as winning a soul.
Because behind many theological questions about sexuality is a human being.
Sometimes frightened.
Sometimes confused.
Sometimes wounded.
Sometimes genuinely searching.
Sometimes desperately hoping God will approve what the heart already wants.
And sometimes quietly terrified that He will not.
So before we go any further, hear this:
Jesus did fulfill the Law.
Completely.
Gloriously.
Perfectly.
But “Jesus fulfilled the Law” does not mean, “Therefore nothing God ever revealed about holiness matters anymore.”
Jesus Himself said:
“Μὴ νομίσητε ὅτι ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὸν νόμον ἢ τοὺς προφήτας· οὐκ ἦλθον καταλῦσαι ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι.”
“Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.”
Matthew 5:17.
The crucial Greek word is πληρῶσαι — plērōsai, from plēroō: to fulfill, fill up, bring to completion.
And notice the word Jesus deliberately contrasts it with:
καταλῦσαι — katalysai.
To tear down. Destroy. Demolish. Abolish.
Jesus is not announcing that God's previous revelation was embarrassing and He had arrived to erase it.
He is declaring that it reaches its intended fulfillment in Him.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christians do not approach Moses as though Jesus never came.
But neither do Christians approach Jesus as though Moses never existed.
We read the whole story through Christ.

The Torah revealed God's holiness, exposed human sin, formed Israel as God's covenant people, anticipated realities ultimately fulfilled in Christ, and carried Israel through a particular covenant administration.
Then Jesus came.
Not as another lamb standing beside the altar.
As the Lamb.
Not as another priest repeating sacrifices.
As the One to whom the sacrifices were pointing.
Not merely as another teacher interpreting God's revelation.
As the Son in whom God's redemptive purposes reach their climax.
That is why the New Testament can say things that initially seem almost contradictory.

Galatians says the Law functioned as a guardian until Christ, and that with the coming of faith God's people are no longer under that guardian. Hebrews speaks explicitly of the new covenant and describes the former covenant as obsolete.
So Christians are not ancient Israelites living under the Sinai covenant.
We do not rebuild the Levitical priesthood.
We do not return to animal sacrifices.
We do not seek justification by keeping Torah.
We do not pretend Calvary never happened.
But here comes the part that makes the question intensely personal.
When the apostles brought the Gospel to Gentiles—people who had never lived as Jews under the Mosaic covenant—they did not conclude:
“Jesus fulfilled the Law, therefore sexual conduct no longer matters.”
Quite the opposite.

At the Jerusalem Council, while explicitly refusing to require Gentile converts to take on the whole Mosaic covenant as the means of belonging to God's people, the apostles still instructed them to abstain from πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
The Greek of Acts 15:20 contains the unmistakable phrase:
“ἀπέχεσθαι … τῆς πορνείας”
—to abstain from sexual immorality.
That should make us stop.
Because these are Gentile Christians.
This is after the resurrection.
After the cross.
After Christ fulfilled the Law.
And sexual holiness did not disappear.
Paul tells the Thessalonian believers:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας”
“For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
1 Thessalonians 4:3.
Read that slowly.
Your sanctification.
Not your humiliation.
Not God's attempt to make you miserable.
Not God's embarrassment over the human body.
Sanctification.
Being made holy.
Belonging increasingly and visibly to God.
This is where many modern conversations go wrong.
We ask:
“How close can I get to the boundary without technically sinning?”
The New Testament asks something far more beautiful and far more terrifying:
“How completely can this body belong to Christ?”
That changes the conversation.
Christian sexual ethics are not ultimately built upon disgust for the body.
They are built upon the breathtaking value God gives the body.
Paul does not tell Christians that their bodies are worthless.
He says something almost shocking:
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
There it is.
The Gospel enters the bedroom.
Not because Jesus is obsessed with catching people doing something dirty.
Because Jesus purchased the whole person.
Your Sunday morning belongs to Him.
Your bank account belongs under His lordship.
Your anger belongs under His lordship.
Your ambitions belong under His lordship.
Your mouth belongs under His lordship.
Your phone belongs under His lordship.
Your sexuality belongs under His lordship.
Your body belongs under His lordship.
Grace never meant:
“Jesus forgave me, therefore my body is irrelevant.”
Grace means something infinitely greater:
“Jesus bought me, therefore even my body can become an instrument of worship.”
And this is why simplistic arguments about “Old Testament sexual laws” often fail.

Leviticus 18 does contain sexual prohibitions. It forbids various incestuous unions, adultery, child sacrifice in connection with Molech, male-male intercourse, and bestiality, among other prohibited practices. The chapter also portrays these practices as defiling and connects them not only with Israel but with the nations occupying the land before Israel.
But Christians should not simply grab Leviticus, ignore the covenantal storyline, and declare the interpretive work finished.
We must ask what happens after Christ comes.
Does the New Testament reaffirm sexual holiness?
Yes.
Does it continue to condemn porneia?
Repeatedly.
Does the apostolic church tell Gentile Christians to abstain from sexual immorality?
Yes.
Does Paul apply an Old Testament sexual boundary involving a man's father's wife directly to a Christian congregation?

Yes. In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul condemns a relationship involving “his father's wife,” showing that at least some sexual boundaries known from Torah remain morally relevant in apostolic Christian instruction.
Does the New Testament teach that keeping Mosaic Law earns salvation?
No.
That is the distinction we desperately need.
A Christian does not refuse sexual sin in order to purchase salvation.
A Christian pursues holiness because salvation has been purchased by Christ.
Those are completely different religions.
One says:
“Obey so God might accept you.”
The Gospel says:
“In Christ, you have been received by grace; now learn to live as someone who belongs to Him.”
One produces pride when you succeed and despair when you fail.
The other produces gratitude, repentance, dependence, and transformation.
And perhaps this is where the conversation stops being theological and becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe you did not click this article because you wanted a lesson about Greek verbs.
Maybe there is a name in your head right now.
A relationship.
A habit.
A night you cannot erase.
A secret.
Maybe you already crossed boundaries you once promised God you never would.
Maybe you have been sleeping beside someone while quietly wondering whether Jesus approves.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to consume bodies while nobody in church knows.
Maybe your marriage has become sexually cold, and temptation suddenly feels less theoretical.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to shame you so brutally that whenever Christians speak about sexual holiness, you hear condemnation before you hear Jesus.
Maybe you are carrying sexual wounds that were inflicted upon you rather than chosen by you.
Hear this distinction carefully:
Being sinned against is not the same as committing the sin done against you.
Someone else's violation does not make you spiritually contaminated beyond Christ's reach.
And if you were abused, exploited, assaulted, manipulated, or coerced, the Gospel does not ask you to carry the perpetrator's guilt as though it belonged to you.
Jesus is not standing over wounded people saying,
“Disgusting.”
He is the Savior who touched people society would not touch.
The Savior who ate with sinners.
The Savior who confronted hypocrisy.
The Savior who spoke truth without needing cruelty.
The Savior who called people to repentance while opening His arms to repentant sinners.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because Jesus neither tells us that sin does not matter nor tells sinners that they are beyond redemption.
He does something far more astonishing.
He takes sin seriously enough to die for it.
And loves sinners deeply enough to die for them.
That is Calvary.
Truth without grace becomes a hammer in human hands.
Grace without truth becomes permission to remain imprisoned.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
He does not save us by pretending darkness is light.
He enters our darkness and leads us out.
That means repentance is not God demanding that you destroy yourself.
Repentance is turning toward the One who came to rescue you.
And yes...
sometimes repentance hurts.
Sometimes following Jesus means surrendering something that feels woven into your identity.
Sometimes obedience means deleting a number.
Ending a relationship.
Confessing to your spouse.
Installing accountability.
Leaving the room.
Closing the browser.
Calling a pastor.
Seeking wise Christian counseling.
Admitting that what you called “freedom” has actually been mastering you.
Sometimes discipleship feels like death because Jesus really does call us to take up a cross.
But Christianity has never taught that every desire inside us automatically possesses moral authority simply because we experience it intensely.
Every disciple eventually discovers desires that must be surrendered.
Sexual desires.
Financial desires.
Desires for revenge.
Desires for status.
Desires for control.
Desires for applause.
Desires for comfort.
Desires to hate.
Desires to hide.
The question is not merely:
“What do I desire?”
The deeper Christian question is:
“Who is Lord of what I desire?”
And the answer cannot be Moses.
It cannot be your pastor.
It cannot be your denomination.
It cannot be your political tribe.
It cannot be social media.
It cannot even be your feelings.
For the Christian, the answer is Jesus Christ.
That does not make biblical interpretation easy.

Sincere Christians and Christian traditions have disagreed over precisely how Old Testament commands should be categorized and applied under the new covenant. The familiar categories of moral, ceremonial, and civil law can be useful theological tools, but the Bible itself does not present Leviticus with modern headings marking every command with those three labels.
So humility matters.
Context matters.
Biblical theology matters.
Jesus matters.
The apostles matter.
We should neither flatten the covenants into one nor cut the Old Testament away from Christian Scripture.
We follow the storyline all the way to Christ.
And when we do, something becomes difficult to escape:
The New Testament does not lower the significance of sexual holiness after Jesus.
It roots holiness more deeply in union with Jesus.
Paul's argument is not merely:
“Moses prohibited something.”
His argument becomes:
You belong to Christ.
Your body matters because Christ redeemed you.
Your sexual conduct matters because your body is for the Lord.
Your holiness matters because the Holy Spirit dwells in God's people.
Suddenly the question changes.
Not:
“Can Christians find a technical exemption?”
But:
“Does this glorify the Jesus who bought me with His blood?”
That question reaches places legalism never can.
Because legalism wants the minimum requirement.
Love asks how much of me belongs to Him.
And the Gospel answers:
All of you.
But perhaps you are thinking:
“You don't know what I've done.”
No.
But Jesus does.
“You don't know how many times I've fallen.”
Jesus does.
“You don't know what I watched.”
He knows.
“You don't know who I slept with.”
He knows.
“You don't know the lies.”
He knows.
“You don't know what happened to me.”
He knows that too.
And still the cross stands.
That is the scandal.
The holy Son of God knew exactly what humanity was—and came anyway.

He did not wait for prostitutes, adulterers, addicts, hypocrites, liars, religious frauds, sexually broken people, sexually wounded people, and self-righteous people to become clean enough to approach Him.
He came looking for sinners.
But He loves us too much to make peace with whatever is destroying us.
Grace says:
“Come as you are.”
Discipleship says:
“You cannot remain exactly as you were.”
The cross says both.
Come.
And die.
Come.
And live.
Come with your shame.
Come with your desires.
Come with your history.
Come with your questions.
Come with your confusion.
Come with the thing you are terrified to surrender.
But come to Jesus.
Not to a Jesus redesigned to agree with us.
To the crucified and risen Christ who loves us enough to forgive us and has authority enough to transform us.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to endorse your desires.
Perhaps tonight the prayer becomes:
“Jesus, teach my desires to bow to You.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because He may touch something.
But He may also free something.
And perhaps what you thought would be the funeral of your happiness becomes the beginning of your freedom.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sexual history publicly.
If you need prayer, simply write:

And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual bondage, shame, pornography, adultery, destructive relationships, or years of secret compromise, consider sharing what God has done without exposing details that should remain private.
Someone reading the comments may believe they are the only person Jesus could never restore.
Your testimony may become the sentence that keeps them from running away.
Not because everybody needs another religious argument on Facebook.
Someone may be trapped between desire and discipleship.
Someone may believe sexual failure permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may be searching for permission when what their soul actually needs is freedom.
Someone may need to discover that holiness and grace are not enemies.
It does not.
Not because paying Gospel Warrior saves you.
Only Jesus saves.

Christians and churches differ in how they understand tithing under the new covenant, and your responsibility to support your local church and other ministries should be approached prayerfully, faithfully, and according to conscience before God.
But voluntary financial partnership with Gospel ministry is thoroughly compatible with the New Testament pattern of believers generously supporting Gospel work.
If you want your resources to glorify God, prayerfully consider whether supporting this work should become part of your voluntary Christian giving.
Your support helps keep the work moving.
Your share helps this message cross a wall money cannot cross.
Your comment tells another struggling believer, “You are not fighting alone.”
And your prayers matter more than any algorithm ever will.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Send it privately to somebody who needs it.
Because ultimately this article was never merely about sex.
It was about lordship.
It was about what happens when Jesus reaches the one room of our lives where we desperately want the final word.
The question is not whether you have a scandal in your story.
Some scandals are public.
Others have passwords.
Some happened because of what we chose.
Others because of what someone did to us.
Some live in bedrooms.
Some live inside memories.
Some are hidden behind wedding photographs and Sunday smiles.
The question is what happens when the scandal meets Jesus.
Because at the cross, Christ does not merely expose sin.
He pays for sin.
He does not merely command repentance.
He makes restoration possible.
He does not merely tell the sexually broken to become clean.
He gives Himself to make sinners clean.
So bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the desires you understand.
Bring Him the desires you do not understand.
Bring Him the past you cannot rewrite.
Then watch what happens when the Author of resurrection takes the pen.
Your past may explain the scars—but it does not get to write the final sentence after Jesus takes hold of the story.
